abstract: While ensemble methods have been widely used for robustness against random perturbations (\ie the average case), ensemble approaches for robustness against adversarial perturbations (\ie the worst case) have remained elusive despite multiple prior attempts. We show that ensemble methods can improve adversarial robustness to multiple attacks if the ensemble is \emph{adversarially diverse}, which is defined by two properties: 1) the sub-models are adversarially robust themselves and yet 2) adversarial attacks do not transfer easily between sub-models. While at first glance, creating such an ensemble would seem computationally expensive, we demonstrate that an adversarially diverse ensemble can be trained with minimal computational overhead via a Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) model. Specifically, we propose to train a MIMO model with adversarial training ({\emph{MAT}}), where each sub-model can be trained on a different attack type. When computing gradients for generating adversarial examples during training, we use the gradient with respect to the ensemble objective. This has a two-fold benefit: 1) it only requires 1 backward pass and 2) the cross-gradient information between the models promotes robustness against transferable attacks. We empirically demonstrate that {\emph{MAT}} produces an ensemble of models that is adversarially diverse and significantly improves performance over single models or vanilla ensembles while being comparable to previous state-of-the-art methods. On MNIST, we obtain $99.5\%$ clean accuracy and ($88.6\%, 57.1\%,71.6\%$) against $(\ell_\infty, \ell_2, \ell_1)$ attacks, and on CIFAR10, we achieve $79.7\%$ clean accuracy and ($47.9\%, 61.8\%,47.6\%$) against $(\ell_\infty, \ell_2, \ell_1)$ attacks, which are comparable to previous state-of-the-art methods.

# RESILIENCE TO MULTIPLE ATTACKS VIA ADVERSARIALLY TRAINED MIMO ENSEMBLES

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

# ABSTRACT

While ensemble methods have been widely used for robustness against random perturbations (i.e., the average case), ensemble approaches for robustness against adversarial perturbations (i.e., the worst case) have remained elusive despite multiple prior attempts. We show that ensemble methods can improve adversarial robustness to multiple attacks if the ensemble is adversarially diverse, which is defined by two properties: 1) the sub-models are adversarially robust themselves and yet 2) adversarial attacks do not transfer easily between sub-models. While at first glance, creating such an ensemble would seem computationally expensive, we demonstrate that an adversarially diverse ensemble can be trained with minimal computational overhead via a Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) model. Specifically, we propose to train a MIMO model with adversarial training  $(MAT)$ , where each sub-model can be trained on a different attack type. When computing gradients for generating adversarial examples during training, we use the gradient with respect to the ensemble objective. This has a two-fold benefit: 1) it only requires 1 backward pass and 2) the cross-gradient information between the models promotes robustness against transferable attacks. We empirically demonstrate that  $MAT$  produces an ensemble of models that is adversarially diverse and significantly improves performance over single models or vanilla ensembles while being comparable to previous state-of-the-art methods. On MNIST, we obtain  $99.5\%$  clean accuracy and  $(88.6\%, 57.1\%, 71.6\%)$  against  $(\ell_{\infty}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{1})$  attacks, and on CIFAR10, we achieve  $79.7\%$  clean accuracy and  $(47.9\%, 61.8\%, 47.6\%)$  against  $(\ell_{\infty}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{1})$  attacks, which are comparable to previous state-of-the-art methods.

# 1 INTRODUCTION

The arms race between attacks and defenses against DNNs has created a diversity of attack types. These include black-box vs white-box attacks and gradient-based vs gradient-free attacks. Ideally, adversarial robust models would be robust against all types of attack. Many defenses have been developed to protect DNNs from adversarial attacks. For instance, gradient masking [23], input denoising [36, 17], and hidden layer randomization [18], are three techniques that in their time were heralded as strong defense techniques. However, [1, 3, 31] show that all of the above methods fail against adaptive adversaries, i.e., perturbations crafted with full knowledge of the defense measure. Among all attempts to make the deep model resilient, Adversarial Training (AT) [19] has stood the test of time and is regarded as the gold standard for its resilience to white-box adversaries [20]. AT trains the deep models with adversarial examples instead of with benign training examples. Due to its empirical robustness, this method remains state-of-the-art against a wide range of attacks. However, AT suffers from two fundamental drawbacks. First, it is computationally expensive, specifically the method to generate effective AEs. Second, the choice of attack type used during training significantly affects the type of robustness that is observed. For example, previous work [30, 25] shows that the model adversarial trained using the  $\ell_{\infty}$  attack is robust against  $\ell_{1}$  and  $\ell_{2}$  PGD attacks but vulnerable against gradient-free attacks. This phenomenon reveals that the robustness of adversarial training implicitly

masks out the gradient information for  $\ell_1$  and  $\ell_2$  attacks. Previous works [30, 20] try to revise adversarial training by training the model using the worst case of PGD adversarial examples among different attack metrics and achieve better results. MSD [20] revises the Tramér and Boneh's method [30] by calculating  $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_{\infty}$  attacks for each step of PGD iteration and updates with the one that achieves the largest loss. This method achieved better performance against  $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_{\infty}$  attacks. However, though MSD is faster than [30], it still requires three forward passes for each step of the PGD attack, which is about 2.5 times the training time of standard AT. Furthermore, MSD compromises on the clean accuracy more than AT.

As ensemble methods have proven to be effective in robustness to random perturbations (i.e., the average case), one natural idea to improve adversarial robustness is to exploit ensemble methods (or model averaging). Ensemble methods combine the predictions of sub-models based on some vote functions (like averaging or majority vote). Previous attempts of using ensemble methods for adversarial robustness have been shown to be vulnerable under strong adversaries [37, 21, 26, 32, 12]. They mainly failed for two reasons. First, if the ensemble is diverse but the models are weak (i.e., not adversarily robust), an adaptive attack only needs to find a single AE that lies in the intersection of the AE space of the sub-models (i.e., a single worst case), which is easy [12]. Intuitively, this finds a single perturbation that is a "common mistake" across sub-models. Second, adversarial examples are very easy to transfer between similar models, i.e., the adversarial perturbation generated from one sub-model may easily mislead another sub-model especially when they share the similar training set or architecture [22]; and the transferability of attacks remains true even if the sub-models are adversarily robust themselves (see vanilla ensemble models in 4.3 of the experiments). Thus, neither diversity of the models nor adversarial robustness of each of the sub-models by themselves can improve adversarial robustness.

To overcome these two prior failures of ensemble methods, we propose to encourage adversarial diversity which is defined to have two key features simultaneously: 1) adversarial robustness of each sub-model and 2) robustness against transfer attacks between sub-models. Additionally, we would like to do this with minimal computational overhead because AT is already very computationally expensive. Our approach is inspired by a recent work called multi-input-multi-output (MIMO) training [10]. MIMO can train  $M$  sub-models simultaneously to form a diverse ensemble, and crucially the training time of the ensemble is almost the same as that of a single model. In this work, we show that by combining MIMO configuration with AT, it is possible to attain robustness against multiple attack types with an adversarily diverse ensemble, i.e., we can achieve adversarial diversity. The results in  $\S 4.1$  and  $\S 4.2$  show that by sharing model parameters, the sub-models act as an implicit way of bringing adversarial diversity while also remaining robust. Then in  $\S 4.3$ , we present that our MAT adversarily trained with each sub-model bestowing resilience to a particular attack metric leads to robustness against multiple types of perturbations. We achieve robustness accuracy ( $88.6\%$ ,  $57.1\%$ ,  $71.6\%$ ) against  $(\ell_{\infty}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{1})$  attack with epsilon ( $10, 2, 0.3$ ) on MNIST. On CIFAR10 dataset, our model achieves robustness accuracy ( $47.9\%$ ,  $61.8\%$ ,  $47.6\%$ ) against  $(\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{\infty})$  attack with radius ( $12, 0.5, 0.03$ ). Finally, in  $\S 4.4$ , we provide an alternative application that one can utilize our MIMO+AT (MAT) by training the MAT with all sub-models trained with the same attack to strengthen previous AT methods to achieve better adversarial robustness without loss of clean accuracy. We provide three examples in this section as  $\ell_{\infty}$  AT,  $\ell_{2}$  AT, and MSD. We summarize our contributions as follows:

1. We shed light on why prior ensemble methods may fail and hypothesize that ensemble methods can improve adversarial robustness if they are adversarially diverse, which is defined by two properties: 1) the sub-models are adversarially robust themselves and yet 2) adversarial attacks do not transfer easily between sub-models. 2.We propose to use MIMO AT (MAT) to train such an ensemble in a computationally efficient way and discuss how the cross-gradient information between the sub-models during training can increase the robustness to transfer attacks between models. 3. We empirically demonstrate that MAT is adversarially diverse and improves significantly over AT models and vanilla ensembles while being comparable or better than prior state-of-the-art methods for multi-attack robustness. Code and pre-trained models for reproducing our experiments have been uploaded to the anonymized repository https:// github.com/anonymous-lab-ml/mimo-adv/.

# 2 PRELIMINARY

In this section, we review some key concepts related to adversarial examples (AEs), adversarial training (AT), and MIMO structure, which will be used through the rest of paper.

# 2.1 ADVERSARIAL ATTACKS

PGD Attack. These attacks seek a point  $x'$  in a neighborhood of the benign example  $x$  with perturbation  $\delta$ , which maximizes the loss  $\mathcal{L}$ . AE  $x$  is generated as:  $x' = x + \arg \max_{\delta \in \mathcal{B}_{\| \cdot \|_p(\epsilon)}} \mathcal{L}(f_\theta(x + \delta), y^*)$ , where  $\epsilon$  denotes the attack radius,  $f_\theta$  is the DNN with parameter  $\theta$ ,  $y^*$  is the true label. A general PGD attack adopts gradient-type algorithm to iterate on the perturbation  $\delta$  as the following

$$
\delta^ {(t + 1)} = \Pi_ {\mathcal {B} _ {\| \cdot \| _ {p}} (\epsilon)} \left(\delta^ {(t)} + \alpha \cdot \mathcal {V} _ {p} \left(\nabla_ {x} \mathcal {L} \left(f _ {\theta} (x), y ^ {*}\right)\right)\right), \quad \text {w i t h} \quad \mathcal {V} _ {p} (\delta) = \underset {v \in \mathcal {B} _ {\| \cdot \| _ {p}} (1)} {\arg \max } v ^ {\top} \delta . \tag {1}
$$

where  $p$  is the attack metric (usually  $\ell_p$  norm),  $\alpha$  is the step size,  $\Pi$  is the operator projecting the gradient onto the  $\ell_p$  ball with radius  $\epsilon$  (denoted by  $\mathcal{B}_{\| \cdot \|_p}(\epsilon)$ ),  $\mathcal{V}_p$  is the operator mapping the gradient to the steepest descent direction on the  $\ell_p$  ball with radius 1. Note that  $\mathcal{V}_p$  is a fundamentally different operator than  $\Pi$ , and in the case of the  $p = \infty$ ,  $\mathcal{V}_\infty$  reduces to the sign of the gradient (as in the FGSM attack). Intuitively, PGD adversarial attack uses iterate with a fixed step size  $\alpha$  along the steepest direction  $\mathcal{V}_p\left(\nabla_x\mathcal{L}(f_\theta(x), y^*)\right)$ . FGSM [9], BIM [15] and [19] can all be treated as variants of the PGD Attack.

# 2.2 ADVERSARIAL TRAINING

Adversarial Training (AT) is regarded as one of the most practical yet effective methods for defending against adversarial attacks. This has stood the "test of time" through multiple iterations of proposed defenses and attacks that discover vulnerabilities in them. AT seeks to build a robust model against adversarial attacks by producing AEs and injecting them into training data by solving a saddle point optimization problem:

$$
\theta^ {*} = \arg \min  _ {\theta} \sum_ {i} \max  _ {\delta_ {i} \in \mathcal {B} _ {\| \cdot \| _ {p}} (\epsilon)} \mathcal {L} \left(f _ {\theta} \left(x _ {i} + \delta_ {i}\right), y _ {i} ^ {*}\right). \tag {2}
$$

Here  $i$  denote the  $i$ -th batch number of training set  $(x_{i},y_{i}^{*})$ . The inner maximization seeks to find the adversarial directions  $\delta_{i}$  given the current classifier  $f_{\theta}$ , and the outer minimization tries to find the best  $\theta$  to minimize the summation of all batches' loss. PGD AT is widely accepted as a standard approximation of inner maximization methods since it is a universal first-order attack algorithm [19]. Though it roughly needs  $K + 1$  times more computation compared to standard training, PGD-AT remains the de facto standard for AT since it walks the balance between strength of attack and computational cost of generating AEs. The drawback of AT is that solving the inner maximization requires a pre-defined attack metric  $p$ , which only contributes to robustness under  $\ell_p$  attacks. [30]. In this paper, we show how the adversarial robustness can be achieved through AT but crucially, one can generalize the defense to multiple attack types and achieve this at about the exact cost as AT.

# 2.3 MIMO ENSEMBLE

Ensemble methods have been widely used to improve a model's calibration and robustness over out-of-distribution samples by averaging over multiple neural network predictions [10, 34, 35]. However, ensemble over  $M$  deep models (sub-models) is usually  $M$  times more expensive from a computational and a memory standpoint. Furthermore, to improve uncertainty estimation, sub-models often sacrifice individual performance to achieve diversified predictions.

To address the computational drawbacks of vanilla ensembles, [10] proposed an ensemble structure called MIMO Ensemble. It showed a surprising result: the benefits of using multiple predictions can be achieved 'for free' under a single model's forward pass. In particular, they showed that, using a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) configuration, one can utilize a single model's capacity to train multiple sub-models that independently learn the task at hand. Since all the layers are shared except for the input layer and the output layer, this architecture uses only about  $1\%$  more parameters. Training a MIMO model has almost the same time complexity as training a standard model while keeping the sub-models diverse without any special regularization and parameter tuning. During training, MIMO uses gradient method to solve following optimization problem for  $M$  sub-models.

$$
\underset {\theta} {\operatorname {m i n i m i z e}} \sum_ {i} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \mathcal {L} (\underbrace {f _ {\theta} \left(x _ {i , 1} , \dots , x _ {i , M}\right) _ {m}} _ {y _ {i, m}}, y _ {i, m} ^ {*}), \tag {3}
$$

where  $(x_{i,1},\ldots x_{i,M})$  are i.i.d sampled from the training set,  $m\in \{1,\dots ,M\}$  denotes the  $m$ -th subnetwork,  $x_{i,m}$  denotes the input of the  $i$ -th batch for the  $m$ -th subnetwork,  $y_{i,m},y_{i,m}^{*}$  represent the outputs from the model and the ground truth respectively, and  $\mathcal{L}$  is the cross entropy loss. Notice that the overall objective is the summation of each sub-model's loss. The separation structure promotes the sub-models' prediction to be less correlated because the output  $y_{j}$  is independent to  $x_{i}$  when  $i\neq j$ . During testing, the same inputs are copied and fed to all the  $M$  sub-models, then MIMO decides the prediction by averaging  $y_{i,m}$ .

# 3 OUR APPROACH: MAT

Given the weaknesses of prior ensemble methods, we seek an algorithm that produces an adversarially diverse ensemble. We define adversarial diversity as an ensemble where 1) the sub-models are adversarially robust themselves and 2) the sub-models are robust to transfer attacks from other sub-models. To achieve this, we propose to combine MIMO and AT, an approach we call  $MAT$ .

There are two questions to adversarially training an ensemble: 1) What loss function should be used to update the sub-model parameters (e.g., the loss for the single sub-model or the ensemble loss)? and 2) How should adversarial examples be created during training? For the first question, one could just update each sub-model independently using the loss of each sub-model—as is often done in standard ensemble methods. However, the prior MIMO work [10] suggests that taking the gradient with respect to the ensemble loss is actually better for clean accuracy (as well as being more computationally efficient). Thus, we adopt this. The second question about which loss to use for creating adversarial examples during training is a bit trickier. Naively, it would seem that gradients with respect to the sub-models' loss would be the best as in standard AT. However, we will discuss how gradients with respect to the total loss across sub-models actually provides a key benefit of making the models more robust to transfer attacks while also being computationally efficient (which was their original purpose).

# 3.1 NAIVE MIMO ADVERSARIAL TRAINING

The foundation of  $MAT$  is our  $M$ -MIMO adversarial training method. We want to train an ensemble that is adversarially diverse. To encourage diversity, we can use different attack types for each sub-model. For this, we wish to learn network parameters that minimize the sum of losses to the perturbations introduced by each attack. As is common in the literature, and without loss of generality, we will use three PGD attacks  $\ell_1, \ell_2$ , and  $\ell_{\infty}$  to instantiate our network. As a naive approach, we may aim to solve the following problem

$$
\min  _ {\theta} \sum_ {i} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \max  _ {\delta_ {i, m} \in \mathcal {B} _ {\| \cdot \| _ {p _ {m}}} (\epsilon_ {m})} \mathcal {L} \left(\underbrace {f _ {\theta} \left(x _ {i , 1} + \delta_ {i , 1} , \dots , x _ {i , M} + \delta_ {i , M}\right) _ {m}} _ {y _ {i, m} ^ {\prime}}, y _ {i, m} ^ {*}\right). \tag {4}
$$

For each batch  $i$ , the inner maximization seeks to find the worst-case adversarial perturbations  $\delta_{i,m}$  given the current classifier  $f_{\theta}$ . Notice that each subnetwork  $m$  finds its own perturbation  $\delta_{i,m}$  inside different balls  $\mathcal{B}_{\| \cdot \|_{p_m}}(\epsilon_m)$ .

The inner maximization, if solved by the  $K$ -step PGD, for each subnetwork  $m$  the perturbation is updated at iteration  $k + 1$  as follows:

$$
\delta_ {i, m} ^ {(k + 1)} = \Pi_ {\mathcal {B} _ {\| \cdot \| p _ {m}} (\epsilon_ {m})} \left(\delta_ {i, m} ^ {(k)} + \alpha_ {m} \cdot \mathcal {V} \left(\nabla_ {x _ {i, m}} \mathcal {L} \left(y _ {i, m} ^ {\prime}, y _ {i, m} ^ {*}\right)\right)\right). \tag {5}
$$

The outer minimization is general SGD. Notice that the difference of equation 5 and vanilla AT perturbation direction equation 1 lies in that equation 5 allows for different projections for different attack types depending on  $\mathcal{B}_{\| \cdot \|_{pm}}$ , which results in potential robustness over diverse attacks.

# 3.2 ENSEMBLE ADVERSARIAL TRAINING (EAT)

While the naïve approach may produce models that are adversely robust by themselves, it does not encourage robustness to transfer attacks between sub-models and additionally, it is computationally expensive since it requires multiple backward passes  $(M)$  for each loss function.

Therefore, to further improve the adversarial diversity  $MAT$ , and also reduce the computation burden, we propose the ensemble adversarial training (EAT) method. The standard adversarial training, with respect to each sub-model, shown in Equation 2, solves the inner maximization by calculating the gradient of its own loss to the input  $x$ . In our  $MAT$  setting, this requires  $m$  backward propagations. The one step of inner maximization is given by

$$
\delta_ {i, m} ^ {(k + 1)} = \Pi_ {\mathcal {B} _ {\| \cdot \| _ {p _ {m}} (\epsilon_ {m})}} \left(\delta_ {i, m} ^ {(k)} + \alpha_ {m} \cdot \mathcal {V} _ {p _ {m}} \left(\nabla_ {x _ {m}} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \mathcal {L} \left(y _ {i, m} ^ {\prime}, y _ {i, m} ^ {*}\right)\right)\right). \tag {6}
$$

For a single batch  $i$  and sub-model  $j$ ,  $EAT$  approximates the true gradient inside PGD attack up to a gap, which is defined as cross gradients as follows. We introduce two properties of the cross gradients.

$$
\operatorname {c r o s s} \left. \operatorname {g r a d i e n t s} (i, j) \triangleq \nabla_ {x _ {i, j}} \sum_ {m \neq j} \mathcal {L} \left(y _ {i, m} ^ {\prime}, y _ {i, m} ^ {*}\right) = \underbrace {\nabla_ {x _ {i , j}} \sum_ {m = 1} ^ {M} \mathcal {L} \left(y _ {i , m} ^ {\prime} , y _ {i , m} ^ {*}\right)} _ {\text {a p p r o x i m a t e g r a d i e n t}} - \underbrace {\nabla_ {x _ {i , j}} \mathcal {L} \left(y _ {i , j} ^ {\prime} , y _ {i , j} ^ {*}\right)} _ {\text {t r u e g r a d i e n t}}\right). \tag {7}
$$

# Preventing adversarial examples crossing the models.

These cross gradients describe the change of  $y_{j}$  w.r.t the change of  $x_{i}$  locally, where  $i \neq j$ . Though the outer minimization weakens the correlation between the sub-models as we mentioned in Section 2.3, there's a possibility that the adversarial perturbation of  $x_{i}$  could flip the  $j$ -th sub-model. Maximizing over the cross gradients produces adversarial perturbation, namely, cross adversarial examples. Introducing this extra term during training reduces the worst-case correlation between sub-models, which contributes to robustness to the cross AES. Convergence with training. MIMO standard training shows that their design of objective function (equation 3) induces the separation of sub-models, i.e., the sub-model  $i$  will have little impact on the output of sub-model  $j$  ( $i \neq j$ ). This separation structure explains why our method works. It can be validated by Fig. 1, where we observed the cross gradients approaching 0 with more epochs of training. Notice that the final cross

# 4.1 DIVERSITY: ADVERSARIAL TRANSFERABILITY AMONG SUB-MODELS

In this section, we observe how the ensemble sub-models perform against adversarial attacks. To better understand our MAT method, we evaluate MAT against  $\ell_2$  adversarial attacks. The results (Tables 1 and 2) show that our model trained using MAT not only gains multiple robustness by the ensemble adversarial training (EAT), but the sub-models are diverse enough to prevent effective adversarial transferability.

A group of classifiers could benefit from the ensemble if and only if each member is diverse enough. There are several different measures trying to quantify the property [14, 37]. In this experiment, we use standard AT to independently train two models with the exact same network architecture as well as the hyperparameters. We test the success rate of adversarial

# 4.2 ROBUSTNESS OF SUB-MODELS

In this section, we empirically show that our sub-models are robust against  $\ell_{\infty}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{1}$  attacks. The results are summarized in Table 3. We observe that using  $MAT$ , each sub-model is relatively robust against all adversarial examples. Combining the fact that the adversarial examples are harder to transfer between these sub-models as shown above,  $MAT$  achieves the desideratum of adversarial diversity. This includes the property that the overall network achieves better performance compared to the sub-models. The only weak sub-model is sub-model 2, which shows vulnerability against  $\ell_{\infty}$  PGD attack, though, the ensemble classifier still performs better than any individual AT model.

# 4.3 MAIN RESULT

In this section, we present the main results of  $MAT$  against various types of attacks. PGD  $\ell_{\infty}$  attack [19], PGD  $\ell_{2}$  attack, sparse PGD  $\ell_{1}$  attack [30], and Carlini & Wagner  $\ell_{2}$  [5] attacks are four types of gradient-based attacks. We also test the gradient-masking effect of our model by evaluating the robustness performance against gradient-free attacks, namely HopSkipJump attack (HSJ) [6], Boundary attack [2], and Salt and Pepper Noise attack [24]. We also report the robustness over the union of multiple attacks, i.e., all  $\ell_{\infty}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{1}$  attacks. We compare  $MAT$  with several baseline models. First, we have three AT models with attack metric  $\ell_{\infty}, \ell_{2}$ , and  $\ell_{1}$ , respectively. We also evaluate the vanilla ensemble of these three models. We also compare our method with MSD [20], the state-of-the-art defense against multiple perturbations. Our main results on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets are summarized in Table 4 and Table 5.  $MAT$  significantly boosts all the previous methods without extra cost (all the models here share the same hyperparameters and the network structure). For  $\ell_{\infty}$  PGD training,  $MAT$  achieves 95.6% accuracy outperforming AT by 0.7%. For  $\ell_{2}$  PGD AT, our methods also increasing the robust accuracy against  $\ell_{2}$  attacks by 1.3%. We also test  $MAT$  coupled with MSD. The results show that on  $\ell_{\infty}$  attacks and  $\ell_{1}$  attacks, we significantly boost the MSD method by 20.2% and 28.2% respectively. The drawback here is that our method has lower accuracy against  $\ell_{2}$  based attack, which requires further hyperparameter tuning to favor the  $\ell_{2}$  attack relative to the others. # 5 RELATED WORK

Adversarial Attacks. In this paper, we mainly focus on white-box attacks, the strongest kind against deep neural architectures [4]. FGSM [9] introduces a one-step attack which is fast, and addresses the demands of tasks where large amounts of AEs are needed. PGD [19] is an iterative version of FGSM, which is well balanced between computation and performance. PGD attacks are widely used to evaluate DNN models' robustness. C&W attack [5] employs an optimization that minimizes the margin loss  $f$  and distance measured by  $\ell_p$  norm. Generally, FGSM attacks are not powerful enough to provide good robustness in AT, whereas C&W attacks are far too computationally expensive to use in AT. Thus, like most others, we use PGD for generating AEs during AT.

Adversarial Defense. Many defenses have been proposed, with most of them being broken by adaptive attacks [1, 3, 31]. Adversarial Training [19], though expensive in computation, has emerged as the best practical way to create models resilient to white-box attacks. A slew of literature has developed variants of AT differing in the way samples are created [8], the way the models are iterated upon [27, 33], and the way different attacks are combined [30, 20]. Our ensemble method is orthogonal to these approaches and therefore can be combined with these, with varying levels of additional design and engineering effort, such as to design the right combining function across the sub-models.

Adversarial Defense against multiple types of perturbation. [20] tries to build a robust model against multiple perturbations by introducing multiple steepest direction PGD attacks during training; their method ensembles three different attacks into one, called multi steepest direction. Our method instead seeks an ensemble over models. [25] introduces a multiple variational autoencoder to build a model robust to either  $\ell_0$  and  $\ell_2$  or  $\ell_0$  and  $\ell_{\infty}$ . However their method is not easy to apply to larger datasets. [29] proposed a provable defense against all  $\ell_p$  norm with robust radius  $3 - 5$  times smaller than state-of-the-art heuristic defense methods [20]. [16] trains DNNs against imperceptible adversarial examples, which are approximated using DNNs. While it shows robustness against a wide range of attacks, its performance against specific attacks is limited. Our approach MAT outperforms prior solutions in this space, either as we have proven empirically for the latest approach [20] or through the author-published numbers on the same dataset.

# 6 CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION

In this paper, we present an adversarially diverse ensemble method called  $MAT$  in which each sub-model achieves both robustness and diversity. We develop the idea of learning an ensemble via adversarial training (AT) and adapt the structure of a recently discovered MIMO architecture. With our optimization technique called ensemble adversarial training (EAT), we require the same number of forward and backward passes as AT and yet achieve generalized robustness against multiple attack types.

MAT achieves state-of-the-art adversarial robustness and outperforms MIMO (expectedly) [10] and vanilla ensemble of AT, where MIMO shows diversity but not robustness, and vanilla ensemble of AT is robust but not diverse. Furthermore, for defending multiple adversarial examples, we achieve state-of-the-art performance which is comparable to MSD [20], while being computationally superior.

A drawback of our scheme is that if the network size is constrained, it may not have the capacity to accommodate multiple sub-models. Another drawback that is common to most AT methods is that the AE perturbation hyperparameters must be manually selected (we simply use the parameters from MSD [20]). Methods for automatically selecting the best hyperparameters using zero-th order optimization would broaden the applicability of our approach.
